questions.question_text: The term that refers to the neglect of all alternate forms of pleasure apart from alcohol is
questions.explanation:
Salience refers to the neglect of all leisure and other alternate form of pleasures apart from alcohol. One's life revolves around getting
alcohol, storing it, saving money to buy it, making opportunities to drink etc. Narrowing of repertoire: A social drinker may drink in various
situations at various places and may have various drinks of his choice. A dependent drinker will settle into a �xed setting, sticking to one
beverage. This may help him maintain steady level of alcohol in blood without much �uctuation. Note that some widening of repertoire is
inevitable in the career of an alcohol drinker - moving from weekends only to all days of the week etc.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a feature of type 1 alcoholism, according to Cloninger?
questions.explanation:
Type 1 alcoholism is milieu-limited (i.e., caused by environmental in�uences e.g. living with alcoholics). Thus it can be seen equally in both
males and females. Subjects often experience a sense of loss of control, typical of alcoholism. They lack a strong family history of alcoholism
and do not have high rates of criminality; the habitual use generally starts after 25 years of age.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect?

options.text: The hallucinations usually last less than a week.
Patients with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium.
The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or voices that may be characteristically malign, and threatening.
The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.
These usually appear in persons abusing alcohol for a long time.

correct_answer.text: The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.

questions.explanation:
Alcoholic hallucinosis: The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or voices that may be characteristically malign, and
threatening. The hallucinations usually last less than a week, when patients believe in the hallucinations though afterwards they may realise
the untrue nature. These usually appear in persons abusing alcohol for a long time. Delusions are usually secondary interpretations of the
hallucinations. The patient is usually distressed, anxious, and restless. Unlike DTs those with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium.
As an empirical timescale, hallucinations lasting for more than 6 months should initiate suspicion of other psychoses including
schizophrenia. The hallucinations respond well and rapidly to antipsychotics. The prognosis is good provided that the person remains
abstinent. But the evidence base for treating alcoholic hallucinosis is very poor.

questions.question_text:
Which drug should be given as prophylaxis against irreversible neurological damage in all patients undergoing in-patient alcohol
detoxi�cation?
questions.explanation:
It is generally advised that all patients undergoing in-patient detoxi�cation should be given parenteral thiamine as prophylaxis for
Wernicke's encephalopathy, which can be associated with irreversible amnesic syndrome in some individuals. This is given for 5 days and
may be followed by oral vitamin B compound. The only Parenteral high potency B-complex vitamin therapy licensed in the UK is Pabrinex.
Prophylactic treatments for patients at high risk of Wernicke's encephalopathy should be one pair IM/IV ampoules high potency B-Complex
vitamins (Pabrinex) daily for 3-5 days. Thiamine 200-300 mg IM daily may be given if Pabrinex is unavailable. Ref: The Maudlsey prescribing
guidelines- 10th edition (Pg 295)

questions.question_text: What is considered as a safe limit of weekly alcohol consumption in women?
questions.explanation:
Safe limits for weekly consumption in males is up to 21 U a week; 21 to 49U is considered hazardous; more than 49U a week amounts to
harmful use range. In females - up to 14U a week is safe; 14-35U being hazardous, and more than 35U being harmful.

questions.question_text: The amount of alcohol units in two pints (2 X 568ml) of beer that has a strength of 4% alcohol by volume (ABV) is
questions.explanation:
A simple method is to multiply ABV in % (alcohol by volume) for a drink by the liters consumed. Thus two pints (2 X 568ml) of beer at 4% ABV
contains 1.136 X 4 = 4.5U

questions.question_text: The symptoms of alcohol withdrawal usually subside within
questions.explanation:
In most alcohol dependent individuals the symptoms of alcohol withdrawal are mild to moderate and usually disappear within 5-7 days after
the last drink.

questions.question_text: According to NICE guidelines, opioid detoxi�cation with buprenorphine in an inpatient setting should last for
questions.explanation:
The NICE guidelines indicate, that opioid detoxi�cation in an inpatient setting may take place over a shorter time than in the community
(suggesting 14-21 days for methadone and 7-14 days for buprenorphine) as the supporting element helps the patient to tolerate emerging
withdrawal symptoms. As in the community, a stabilisation on the dose of a substitute opioid is �rst achieved, followed by gradual dose
reduction; with additive medications judiciously prescribed for withdrawal symptoms if and as needed.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is regarded as the most suitable screening tool for the hazardous use of alcohol in primary care settings?
questions.explanation:
A recent systematic review 21 of the literature has concluded that the AUDIT is the best screening instrument for the whole range of alcohol
problems in primary care

questions.question_text: For detecting hazardous and dependent drinking in primary care, which one of the following is recommended as the best tool to use?
questions.explanation:
AUDIT (Alcohol use disorders identi�cation test) is designed to be used as a brief structured interview or self report questionnaire, which is
suitable for general practice use. It has a sensitivity of about 83% among males and 65% among females in primary care settings.

questions.question_text:
A 34-year-old patient who has been dependent on alcohol meets with a road tra�c accident and is admitted at an orthopaedic ward for a
fractured wrist. Which of the following is correct with respect to his clinical state?

options.text: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms usually starts within 48 hours
The chances of having a delirium is highest after 5 days
He will not have a seizure unless he has a head injury
Risk of seizure is maximal from day 3 to day 5.
Having withdrawal symptoms 5 days after abstinence is unusual

correct_answer.text: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms usually starts within 48 hours

questions.explanation:
Withdrawal seizures (rum �ts) occur within 6-48 hours of alcohol cessation; they are major motor seizures that take place during withdrawal
in patients who normally have no seizures and have normal electroencephalograms (EEGs). These seizures are typically generalized and
brief.

questions.question_text: Disul�ram inhibits which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Disul�ram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, thus leading to acetaldehyde accumulation after drinking alcohol, which can cause extremely
unpleasant side e�ects, leading to signs and symptoms such as �ushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, tachycardia and palpitations if alcohol
is consumed Continued drinking can lead to arrhythmias, hypertension and collapse. Therefore, the treating clinician must ensure that no
alcohol has been consumed by patient 24 hours before commencing on treatment.

questions.question_text: Which class of drugs is recognised as the treatment of choice for alcohol withdrawal?
questions.explanation:
Benzodiazepines are recognised as the treatment of choice for alcohol withdrawal. They are cross tolerant with alcohol and have
anticonvulsant properties. They are typically given for seven days. Benzodiazepines are better than placebo for alcohol withdrawal for
various outcomes including reducing the severity of withdrawal, reduction in the incidence of complications (delirium and seizures),
completion of regimen and subsequent rehabilitation. The choice of which benzodiazepine to use depends on the circumstances of
treatment; almost all benzodiazepines are shown to be e�cacious in alcohol detoxi�cation

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is not associated with alcoholism?
questions.explanation: Binswanger's disease is a vascular dementia not directly linked to alcohol use.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the drug of choice in patients with an uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Chlordiazepoxide is the drug of choice in patients with uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal as it has a low dependence forming potential. A
typical �xed regimen for covering uncomplicated withdrawal is 20 mgs q.d.s. of Chlordiazepoxide, reducing over approximately seven days.
Additional titration using prn medication can be used in the �rst two days.

questions.question_text: You are called to A&E to see a man withdrawing from amphetamines. He is least likely to have
questions.explanation:
Amphetamine withdrawal e�ects include dysphoric mood (crash) sometimes with suicidal ideation, fatigue, vivid, unpleasant dreams,
increased appetite and hypersomnia besides psychomotor retardation/agitation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs often require direct supervision by the treating clinician when the treatment is commenced?
questions.explanation:
Disul�ram acts as a deterrent. Disul�ram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, resulting in the accumulation of acetaldehyde leading to signs
and symptoms such as �ushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, tachycardia and palpitations if alcohol is consumed. This reaction is dose-
dependent and if a large amount of alcohol is consumed, a more severe reaction may ensue leading to hypertension, collapse and even
death. Therefore, the prescribing clinician must ensure that no alcohol has been consumed by patient 24 hours before commencing on
treatment. Witnessing, or supervising, the taking of disul�ram is important for its e�cacy. There is little evidence to guide how long patients
should receive disul�ram but, generally, 3-6 months is advocated, or for as long any bene�ts are maintained.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature seen in hepatocerebral degeneration due to alcoholism?
questions.explanation:
Dystonia is not a feature of hepatocerebral degeneration due to alcoholism. Hepatic encephalopathy due to liver failure is characterized by
altered sensorium, frontal release signs, 'metabolic' �apping tremor, hyper-re�exia and extensor plantar responses. High mortality rates are
noted; in those who make a partial recovery, a discrete neurological de�cit characterised by tremor, choreoathetosis, dysarthria, gait ataxia,
and dementia results. This is called as hepatocerebral degeneration. Enlargement and proliferation of protoplasmic astrocytes in the basal
ganglia, thalamus, red nucleus, pons, and cerebellum, in the absence of neuronal loss or other glial changes, is noted.

questions.question_text: Alcohol blocks the consolidation of new memories into old memories through its actions at which of the following brain regions?
questions.explanation: Alcohol blocks the consolidation of new memories into old memories at hippocampus.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a marker for excess alcohol consumption?
questions.explanation:
Increased MCV is a marker for excess alcohol use, with a sensitivity of 20- 50%, and speci�city of 55-100%. It remains raised for 3-6 months,
due to the 120-days lifespan of RBCs. It can turn false positive in patients with B12 or folate de�ciency.  GGT, a liver enzyme, has a sensitivity
of 20- 90%, and speci�city of 55- 100% to detect harmful use of alcohol. It remains raised for 2- 4 weeks.  Other liver function tests are less
speci�c for alcoholic-related liver damage. Elevated GGT can be a false positive �nding in patients with other liver diseases and may remain
raised in chronic alcoholic liver disease despite abstinence. CDT (Carbohydrate de�cient transferase) has a sensitivity of 70%, and speci�city
of 95%. Increased levels of CDT occur in response to heavy drinking. A CDT test is more expensive than GGT test, and not available in some
hospitals. Ref: Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry; 508

questions.question_text: Which of the following alcohol-related neurological damage has a speci�c association with red wine?
questions.explanation:
Marchiafava-Bignami syndrome: It was �rst described by Carducci in 1898 in Italian red wine drinkers and by Marchiafava and Bignami in
1903. It occurs predominantly in malnourished alcoholics and is reported more often in male than female drinkers. Demyelination of the
corpus callosum and adjacent subcortical white matter (Extrapontine myelinolysis) occurs. Dementia, spasticity, dysarthria, gait changes
occur. Patients may lapse into coma and die, survive for many years with a dementia

questions.question_text:
If considering opioid detoxi�cation, women who are pregnant or planning for pregnancy should consider treatment with which one of the
following agents?
questions.explanation:
Women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy should consider treatment with Methadone. Ideally, the mother should be encouraged
to become abstinent prior to delivery--often this may not be possible. If pregnancy begins while a woman is taking high doses of methadone,
the dosage should be reduced slowly (e.g., 1 mg every 3 days), and foetal monitoring must be carried out closely.

questions.question_text:
Mr. X is a 45-year-old gentleman admitted to hospital with features of severe alcohol withdrawal, and laboratory investigations are
arranged. Which one of the following �nding is least likely to be found in his blood test results?
questions.explanation:
When alcohol withdrawal is severe/complicated, it is important to arrange laboratory investigations in order to check for Macrocytosis, Low
haemoglobin, Raised liver function tests, Leucocytosis and Thrombocytopenia. It is also important to check for dehydration, hyponatraemia,
hypokalemia, hypomagnesaemia, also hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia. Ref: The Maudlsey prescribing guidelines- 10th edition (Pg 287)

questions.question_text:
Mr. X is a 45-year-old gentleman being treated with methadone for opioid dependence and recently took an overdose of methadone. Which
drug should be administered in the event of methadone overdose?
questions.explanation:
In the event of methadone overdose, Naloxone should be administered following BNF Guidelines. It may be given by intravenous,
intramuscular or subcutaneous routes. The emergency services should always be called. 0.4-2 mg repeated at intervals of 2-3 minutes to a
maximum of 10 mg should be tried. Naloxone is short acting, and the e�ect may reverse within 20 minutes to 1 hour, meaning that a patient
can revert back into an overdose state. Therefore an ongoing medical monitoring should be provided after Naloxone administration.

questions.question_text:

drink only at home sticking to vodka. He is exhibiting
questions.explanation:
Narrowing of repertoire: A social drinker may drink in various situations at various places and may have various drinks of his choice. A
dependent drinker will settle into a �xed setting, sticking to one beverage. This may help him maintain a steady level of alcohol in the blood
without much �uctuation. Note that some widening of repertoire is inevitable in

questions.question_text:
A 40-year-old woman with signi�cant alcohol-related problems does not recognise her responsibility or requirement to change her lifestyle.
She even denies that her problems are alcohol related. She is in which of the following stages of change?
questions.explanation:
During the precontemplation stage, patients do not even consider changing. Smokers who are in denial may not see that the advice applies
to them personally. Patients with high cholesterol levels may feel "immune" to the health problems that strike others. Obese patients may
have tried unsuccessfully so many times to lose weight that they have simply given up (Retrieved from

questions.question_text:
Which of the following feature is suggestive of schizophrenia instead of alcoholic hallucinosis in patients who have psychotic symptoms in a
background of alcoholism?

options.text: Onset of alcohol drinking clearly preceding the onset
Remission of psychotic episodes during abstinence
Atypical or late age of onset of psychotic symptoms
Presence of thought disorder and a�ect incongruence.
Recurrence of hallucinations when drinking pattern is reinstated

correct_answer.text: Presence of thought disorder and a�ect incongruence.

questions.explanation:
When considering alcoholic hallucinosis, di�erences from schizophrenia include atypical or late age of onset of psychotic symptoms, the
onset of alcohol drinking clearly preceding the onset, remission of psychotic episodes during abstinence and lack of thought disorder and
a�ect incongruence.

questions.question_text:
Mr. X is a patient, who is alcohol abstinent for a long time but went back to the original pattern of heavy drinking in a surprisingly rapid
manner after having a priming dose of alcohol. This state is described as;
questions.explanation:
Reinstatement on relapse: This is a criterion stressed by Edward and Gross in their early description of alcohol dependence. A patient, who
is abstinent for a long time, may go back to the original pattern of heavy drinking in a surprisingly rapid manner after having a priming dose
of alcohol (relapse). Various explanations for this include: 1. abstinence violation e�ect - the cognition that 'I had a drink; so I am a drinker
again' may force patients to reinstate full pattern of drinking 2. propensity to experience withdrawal symptoms may be carried over even
through the period of abstinence in some individuals 3. Cues may trigger memory after priming dose, making compulsive drinking a
behaviour

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a feature of type II alcoholism, according to Cloninger?
questions.explanation:
The features of type II alcoholism includes inheritance of the condition from the father, onset of alcohol-related problems before the age of
25 years, being found primarily  in males, prominent history of criminality and poor prognosis characterized by an inability to achieve
meaningful abstinence.

questions.question_text: Diminished or reverse tolerance is associated with all of the following except

options.text: Metabolic problems such as liver disease
When drinking alcohol after a period of abstinence

questions.explanation:
Diminished tolerance is a notable phenomenon in drinkers. When drinking alcohol after a period of abstinence, the tolerance may revert to
normal and might lead to quick intoxication. Older patients with brain damage may have curtailed neuroadaptation leading to reversed
tolerance. Metabolic problems such as liver disease may apparently look like diminished tolerance.It may also be idiosyncratic in certain
individuals.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following drugs used to prevent relapse of alcohol use appears to act centrally on glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter
system?
questions.explanation:
Acamprosate is a synthetic taurine analogue, which appears to act centrally on glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter system. It is licensed
to prevent relapse in alcohol use and has been found to have modest treatment e�ect.

questions.question_text: Sally is 10-weeks pregnant. She is on 70mg methadone daily and wants to stop taking it. What would you advise her to do?

options.text: Reduce and stop over next 2 weeks

questions.explanation:
Women can present with opioid dependency at any stage in pregnancy. Stabilization on substitute methadone is the treatment of choice in
any stage, as it has an established record of safe use in pregnancy. Opioid misuse in pregnancy can cause miscarriage and substitute
prescribing carries a lower risk than continuing opioid misuse. Tapering of methadone is not recommend while someone is pregnant, as it
can add to the chance of relapsing, developing withdrawals, and may precipitate miscarriage. Buprenorphine may be used in pregnancy,
although there is less evidence for this and experts do not at present recommend routinely changing over mid pregnancy to this agent.

Delirium tremens is a toxic confusional state that occurs when alcohol withdrawal symptoms are severe. The symptoms typically peak
between 72-96 hours after the last drink. The classical symptoms include confusion, distraction & clouding of consciousness, vivid
hallucinations a�ecting every sensory modality and marked tremors. Clinical features also include �eeting paranoid delusions, agitation,
sleep disturbances, signs of autonomic hyperactivity such as fever, sweating, tachycardia and hypertension

questions.question_text: Following sudden cessation of alcohol on a dependent patient, the risk of seizure is high during which of the following time periods?
questions.explanation:
As part of alcohol withdrawal symptoms, generalized seizures rarely occur , usually within 24 hours of cessation from alcohol.
Benzodiazepines especially long-acting ones such as diazepam reduce the risk of seizures.

questions.question_text:
A man who repeatedly presents to A& E with his girlfriend who is pregnant and heavy abuser of heroin. She plans to breast-feed following
childbirth. Which medication is preferable to continue if she starts breast feeding
questions.explanation:
Methadone is considered compatible with breast-feeding. The Clinical Guidelines recommend that breast feeding should still be
encouraged, but that with regards to methadone and breast feeding "the dose is kept as low as possible while maintaining stability, and the
infant monitored to avoid sedation. (Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines- 316)

questions.question_text:
A man after completing his opioid detoxi�cation is highly motivated to remain on treatment and wants advice about maintaining it. Which of
the following drugs is best suited in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Naltrexone is recommended as a treatment option in detoxi�ed, formerly opioid dependent subjects who are highly motivated to remain in
an abstinence programme. For this group naltrexone treatment has been found by NICE to be a cost e�ective treatment strategy in aiding
abstinence from opioid misuse. (www.nice.org.uk- Technology appraisal 115, 2007)

questions.question_text: Tim is taking heroin regularly. He has been tried unsuccessfully on methadone and buprenorphine. Choose the next best option
questions.explanation:
Current consensus guidelines suggest that patient should have "speci�cally optimised higher dose oral methadone or buprenorphine
maintenance treatment" after oral maintenance therapy (i.e. option B, then option A) before moving on to injectables. Injectable heroin and
methadone treatments should be considered only for the minority of patients who are genuinely unresponsive to an optimised oral
maintenance treatment approach. Injectable and oral substitute prescribing must be supported by locally commissioned and provided
mechanisms for supervised consumption. Injectable drugs may present more risk of overdose than oral preparations and have a greater
value on illicit markets and hence may require greater levels of supervision.
(Ref:www.nta.nhs.uk/uploads/nta_injectable_heroin_and_methadone_2003_fullguide.pdf)

questions.question_text:
Tom is on methadone treatment for heroin addiction. He attends A&E on two occasions as he is "running out of supply of methadone" and
demands treatment. What is the best course of action?
questions.explanation:
It is possible that he is experiencing withdrawal symptoms, due to inadequate dose of methadone and possibly self medicating himself. The
best course of action is to stabilise this patient by optimizing the dose of methadone. It is inadvisable to issue additional replacement
opiates from the A&E Department. Liaising and passing on this information to the local drug service is what is essential so that they can
review their prescribing and possibly increase the daily dose with closer supervision.

questions.question_text:
Sally is physically dependent on dihydrocodeine, which she is taking for back pain. She wants to stop this and go back to work. What is the
best course of action?
questions.explanation:
Withdraw codeine cautiously in �rst instance, in conjunction with other pain management approaches (eg pregabalin, SNRI, psychology,
TENS) and if unsuccessful then consider changing to methadone to facilitate withdrawal.

questions.question_text:
The risk of developing alcohol problems for those with a positive family history compared to those without a family history of alcohol
problems is increased by
questions.explanation: The risk of alcoholism in relatives of alcoholic probands is nearly four times as high as that of the general population. (Dawson et al. 1992)

questions.question_text:
A patient is keen to come o� heroin use but is anxious about experiencing withdrawal symptoms. Which of the following is best suited to
support detoxi�cation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Methadone treatment is more successful if carried out slowly or with a linear dose reduction; methadone can suppress withdrawal for 24 -
36 hours so once daily dosing is su�cient. Methadone may be desired by patients who do not want any withdrawal discomfort and/or
anxious of experiencing a di�cult withdrawal.

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients with schizophrenia smoke?
questions.explanation:
A quantitative review of 42 studies from 20 countries reported a 62% pooled rate of smoking in patients with schizophrenia, which was
signi�cantly elevated relative to general population (weighted average odds ratio, OR = 5.9; males = 7.2; females = 3.3) and psychiatric
comparison groups (OR: 1.9). de Leon, J., and Diaz, F. J. (2005). A meta-analysis of worldwide studies demonstrates an association between
schizophrenia and tobacco smoking behaviors. Schizophrenia Research, 76(2-3), 135-157. Compare these rates with the fact that only one-
third of the general population smokes at any given time. In schizophrenia the possible explanations for higher rates of smoking are as
follows; 1. Smoking causes dopamine release, leading to feelings of well-being and a reduction in negative symptoms; 2. Alleviation of some
of the side e�ects of antipsychotics such as drowsiness, EPSEs and cognitive slowing, 3. As a means of structuring the day or 4. As a means
of alleviating the de�cit in auditory gaiting that is found in schizophrenia. Cigarette smoking in schizophrenia, relationship to
psychopathology and medication side e�ects, Am J Psychiatry 1992; 149; 1189-1194

questions.question_text:
A 35-year-old man states that he is currently drinking two bottles of wine a day. He is unable to cut down due to symptoms of insomnia,
agitation and tremors. He is also reported to su�er from low mood, anhedonia and fatiguability. What would be the most appropriate
treatment option?
questions.explanation:
Alcohol detoxi�cation is the most appropriate option to be tried �rst. Many alcohol withdrawal episodes take place without any medical or
pharmacological treatment. In alcohol detoxi�cation, the intended goals can be symptom suppression, avoiding complications and
completion of regimen with subsequent abstinence. Community-based detoxi�cation involves daily contact with a nurse to assess
withdrawal and monitor for complications.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a mechanism of action of Acamprosate in treating alcohol dependence?
questions.explanation: Acamprosate restores the altered balance between inhibitory and excitatory system seen in alcohol dependence.

questions.question_text:
A 55-year-old gentleman, with a history of opioid dependence, would like to consider pharmacological maintenance treatment along with
psychosocial interventions. The most appropriate medication would be;
questions.explanation:
For all patients who are opioid dependent with an informed decision to become abstinent, services should readily o�er detoxi�cation. O�er
buprenorphine or methadone as �rst line treatment, with due consideration to service user's preference.

questions.question_text: Which of the following screening tools have only four questions?
questions.explanation: CAGE has only 4 questions. AUDIT has 10 questions.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following substance is likely to be an active ingredient in the Ethiopian plant Catha edulis, whose leaves on chewing provide
amphetamine-like stimulation?
questions.explanation:
The stimulant e�ect of the Khat plant was originally attributed to cathine, but this was disputed by reports showing the plant extracts from
fresh leaves contained another substance more active than cathine - called cathinone. Cathinone is not very stable and breaks down to
produce cathine and norephedrine. This explains why fresh leaves are more stimulating, and the habit of chewing Khat is often con�ned to
the regions where it is cultivated.

questions.question_text:
Mr. P has a long standing history of substance misuse and has developed an ischaemic cerebrovascular disorder. Which of the following
substance is most likely to precipitate it?
questions.explanation:
The major complications of chronic use are cerebrovascular, epileptic and cardiac. The most common cerebrovascular diseases associated
with cocaine use are non-haemorrhagic cerebral infarctions. When haemorrhagic infarctions do occur, they can include subarachnoid,
intraparenchymal and intraventricular haemorrhages. Other adverse e�ects of cocaine use include seizures, myocardial infarctions and
arrhythmias. Ref: Kaplan and Sadock Synopsis of Psychiatry 9th edition; Pg 434.

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms is least suggestive of an opioid withdrawal state?
questions.explanation:
Opioid withdrawal is rarely fatal in a healthy adult. Morphine and heroin withdrawal syndrome begins 6 to 8 hours after the last dose, peaks
in 2 days and reduces in a week usually. The features include dysphoric mood, nausea or vomiting, muscle aches, lacrimation or rhinorrhea,
pupillary dilation, piloerection (goose �esh), or sweating, diarrhea, yawning, fever and insomnia. Note that insomnia, bradycardia,
temperature dysregulation, and a craving for opioids can persist for months after an episode of withdrawal, necessitating maintenance
methadone in number of patients.

questions.explanation:
This patient is currently contemplating a change in behaviour. During the contemplation stage, patients are ambivalent about changing.
Giving up an enjoyed behavior causes them to feel a sense of loss despite the perceived gain. During this stage, patients assess barriers (e.g.,
time, expense, hassle, fear, "I know I need to, doc, but ...") as well as the bene�ts of change (Retrieved from

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most common during cocaine withdrawal?
questions.explanation:
E�ects of cocaine are short-lived with a rapid cessation of physiological e�ects occurring due to a rapid metabolism; this can induce a
pattern of repeated use. Dysphoria (crash), anhedonia, anxiety, irritability hypersomnolence, and sometimes agitation usually end within 18
hours though in heavy dependent users this can last up to a week, peaking in 3 days. The characteristic feature is intense cravings for
cocaine with a striking lack of much physical withdrawal symptoms.

questions.question_text: In Korsako� syndrome, the type of memory that is most a�ected is
questions.explanation:
Korsako�'s is characterized by marked de�cits in anterograde and to some extent retrograde episodic memory, apathy, an intact sensorium,
and relative preservation of other intellectual abilities such as attention, procedural memory and working memory. An impairment in the
physiological processes assumed to underlie the storage (consolidation) of information in a more permanent form ( the 'transfer' of
information from primary to secondary memory), is proposed. Consistent with this hypothesis, digit span test scores and other measures of
working memory are characteristically intact in patients with Korsako�'s syndrome. Kopelman, M. D., et al (2009). The Korsako� Syndrome:
Clinical Aspects, Psychology and Treatment. Alcohol Alcohol., 44(2), 148-154.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a common criterion for both 'substance abuse' and 'substance dependence' categories in diagnostic classi�cations?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis of substance abuse is based on the consequences in physical, psychological, social and occupational aspects of a person's life.
To diagnose dependence other criteria must also be met in addition to the impairment criteria.

questions.question_text: The route of cocaine administration that can produce a 'high' that can last up to 15 to 30 minutes is
questions.explanation:
The duration of cocaine's euphoric e�ects ('high') depends upon the route of administration. The faster the absorption, the more intense the
'high'. The faster the absorption, the shorter the duration of action. The euphoria resulting from snorting is relatively slow in onset, and may
last 15 to 30 minutes while that from smoking or mainlining may last 5 to 10 minutes. Inhalation (smoking) or intravenous injections cause a
very rapid onset of action.

questions.question_text:
A man who has been abusing multiple substances now complains of frequent urination and passing blood in the urine. The most likely
o�ending drug is;
questions.explanation:
Ketamine is a derivative of phencyclidine, a popular street drug that is known as 'PCP' or 'angel dust'. Ketamine is less potent, and shorter
acting compared with phencyclidine and is used as a dissociative anaesthetic in humans. The e�ects of ketamine include profound changes
in consciousness and psychotomimetic symptoms, such as out-of-body experiences. Negative e�ects include increased heart and
respiratory rates, nausea and vomiting, convulsions, temporary paralysis and hallucinations [2]. So far only one report has described the

Lifetime prevalence of any psychiatric disorders is 80%

At least 60-80% of cocaine users admit to mental health problems at some point when surveyed. Among these 18-20% have psychotic

questions.question_text: Among the following list, the drug least likely to cause physical or psychological dependence is
questions.explanation:
Both physical and psychological dependence on hallucinogens are rare and not seen in present day clinical practice. This may be due to lack
of reliable euphoria from hallucinogen use. Cannabis, on other hand, causes well established psychological dependence. Physical
dependence is rare in average users.

questions.explanation:
Opioid withdrawal symptoms may include lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, agitation, perspiration, piloerection, vomiting, shivering, yawning and
dilated pupils. Muscle spasms and twitching are signs of advanced opioid withdrawal state.

questions.question_text: Identify the correct statement regarding treatment with naltrexone?

options.text: Fatal overdose in those who relapse is rare
It has a much shorter half life than Naloxone
Prior to giving the drug, patients should be advised of the risk of withdrawal
Combining naltrexone with psychological interventions provides limited additional bene�t over naltrexone alone
Its e�ectiveness as a treatment for relapse prevention in opiod misusers is con�rmed

correct_answer.text: Prior to giving the drug, patients should be advised of the risk of withdrawal

questions.explanation:
Naltrexone has a longer half-life than Naloxone. The evidence base to support the use of naltrexone for opioid relapse prevention is
currently inadequate. Naltrexone might precipitate serious withdrawal syndrome if prescribed in an ongoing heroin user and therefore
patients should be advised of the risk of withdrawal, prior to giving the drug. Close monitoring is particularly important when naltrexone
treatment is initiated because of the higher risk of a fatal overdose at this time.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a feature of opioid withdrawal?
questions.explanation:
Signs and symptoms of opioid withdrawal syndrome include yawning, sweating, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, anxiety, restlessness, insomnia,
dilated pupils, piloerection, chills, tachycardia, hypertension, nausea/vomiting, crampy abdominal pains, diarrhoea, and muscle aches and
pains. Unlike withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines, opioid withdrawal is not life threatening. The emergence of withdrawal
symptoms varies with the half-life of the speci�c opioid substance; within 6-12 hours after the last dose of morphine or 72-96 hours
following methadone. Duration and intensity of withdrawal symptoms can be variable and are related to clearance of the drug; withdrawal
from morphine is short (5-10 days) but more protracted with methadone

questions.question_text: Which of the following could be used as a replacement therapy for a heroin user?
questions.explanation:
Suboxone contains buprenorphine as well as the opioid antagonist naloxone to deter the abuse of tablets by intravenous injection.
Controlled trials suggest that buprenorphine and naloxone at a 4:1 ratio will produce unpleasant withdrawal symptoms if taken
intravenously by patients who are addicted to opioids, but has no such e�ect when taken sublingually. However, Suboxone formulation still
has the potential to produce an opioid agonist "high" if injected by non-dependent persons. Suboxone is approved by the European
regulating body.

questions.question_text:
A 60-year-old lady with long standing history of alcoholism presents with ataxia, nystagmus and confusion. She was admitted to the medical
ward. Which one among the following drugs should be used as prophylaxis in the further management of this case?
questions.explanation:
This case has developed Wernicke's Encephalopathy due to alcohol misuse. It is advised that all patients undergoing in-patient detoxi�cation
should be given parenteral thiamine (Vitamin B1) as prophylaxis for Wernicke's Encephalopathy. This is probably given for �ve days and may
be followed by oral vitamin B compound. Intravenous Pabrinex (only parenteral high potency B complex vitamin therapy licensed in UK)
remains the treatment of choice in patients in whom a diagnosis of WE has been made or for whom the diagnosis is clear. (Ref: The
Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines- 10th edition-pg 295)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about the pharmacokinetics of alcohol?

options.text: Females have less risk of intoxication for the same units consumed when compared to males
Drinks with more than 30% alcohol content are absorbed more readily than those with less concentration
Reduced gastric motility increases alcohol absorption
Most alcohol is excreted unchanged in urine
Pyloric stenosis decreases the absorption of alcohol

correct_answer.text: Pyloric stenosis decreases the absorption of alcohol

questions.explanation:
The longer alcohol is exposed to gastric alcohol dehydrogenase greater will be its breakdown (and consequently less the blood levels). As a
result, the presence of pyloric stenosis may reduce the chances of a rapid overshoot of alcohol in blood and intoxication. Most alcohol is
broken down by the liver (85%). A small proportion (2-5%) of the alcohol absorbed is excreted unchanged in the urine, sweat or breath.
Females have a higher risk of intoxication as they have only 50% of alcohol dehydrogenase that is seen in the gastric mucosa of men. Drinks
with an alcohol content between 20-30% are absorbed quickest. Drinks with a further high alcohol content are absorbed more slowly as an
alcohol content over 30% irritates the gastric mucosa, stimulates mucus secretion and reduces gastric emptying.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect?

options.text: Patients with alcoholic hallucinosis have a clear sensorium.
These usually appear in persons abusing alcohol for a long time
The hallucinations usually last less than a week, when patients believe in the hallucinations though afterwards they may realise the
The most common hallucinations are unstructured sounds or voices that may be characteristically malign, and threatening.
The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.

correct_answer.text: The hallucinations respond poorly to antipsychotics.

questions.explanation:
In alcoholic hallucinosis (AH), the hallucinations respond well and rapidly to antipsychotics. The prognosis is good provided that the person
remains abstinent. AH can be treated with oral haloperidol, but caution is needed as haloperidol can reduce seizure threshold.
